candidates.title: Bone marrow stimulation improves 12-month clinical outcomes after isolated meniscal repair: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.
candidates.authors_short: Pakmanee N, Limitlaohaphan C, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare short-term clinical outcomes and meniscal healing on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 12 months between standard arthroscopic meniscal repair and repair augmented with bone marrow stimulation (BMS) in isolated meniscal tears. METHODS: In this prospective, two-centre, double-blind randomized controlled trial, patients aged 18-60 years with an isolated meniscal tear confirmed on MRI were randomized 1:1 to standard repair or repair augmented with BMS. Medial, lateral and bicompartmental tears were included. The primary outcome was the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective score at 12 months. Secondary outcomes were the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), Lysholm score, Tegner activity scale, pain on a visual analogue scale (VAS), patient satisfaction, operative time, adverse events and meniscal healing on 12-month MRI (3.0-T) (Crues classification, two-blinded assessors). RESULTS: Fifty patients (mean age 40.2 years; 21 male and 29 female) were randomized; all completed follow-up. Baseline characteristics were balanced; the augmented group received significantly more sutures (4.2 ± 1.4 vs. 3.3 ± 1.1; p = 0.011) and had fewer horizontal tears (44% vs. 76%; p = 0.042). At 6 months, Lysholm and satisfaction scores already favoured the augmented group. At 12 months, it was superior for the IKDC score (82.5 ± 12.6 vs. 56.5 ± 18.5), WOMAC score (14.6 ± 20.0 vs. 41.8 ± 32.5), Lysholm score (91.8 ± 6.4 vs. 72.6 ± 17.2), Tegner activity scale (median 5.0, interquartile range [IQR] 4.0-6.0 vs. 3.0, IQR 2.0-4.0), pain (0.6 ± 0.7 vs. 2.3 ± 2.3) and satisfaction (9.7 ± 0.6 vs. 7.9 ± 1.7); all p < 0.05. MRI healing did not differ between groups (p = 0.783; unhealed: 2/25 [8%] per group); operative time was similar, and no complications occurred within 12 months. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, BMS augmentation was associated with superior patient-reported outcomes at 12 months, without additional complications or an increase in operative time. Meniscal healing on MRI did not differ between groups. These positive short-term findings helped to prove the benefit of BMS augmentation, although confirmation in larger trials with longer follow-up and structural assessment is required to clarify the effectiveness, durability and indications of BMS. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic randomized controlled trial.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality RCT from a reputable journal examining bone marrow stimulation augmentation for meniscal repair with strong design (double-blind RCT), meaningful clinical outcomes, and statistically significant improvements in IKDC, WOMAC, and Lysholm scores at 12 months.
bullets: Adding bone marrow stimulation to meniscal repair produced significantly better pain, function, and activity scores at 12 months compared to repair alone in adults aged 18 to 60 with isolated meniscal tears.

MRI healing rates at 12 months were the same in both groups (8% unhealed each), suggesting the functional benefit from bone marrow stimulation is not explained by improved structural healing on imaging.

The technique added no extra operative time and no complications, making it a low-risk adjunct to consider for isolated meniscal repair, though larger trials with longer follow-up are needed before broad adoption.

candidates.title: Effect of Excision of the Infrapatellar Fat Pad in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Double-Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Howard A, Naeem H, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is frequently excised during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) to improve exposure, but its role in postoperative pain and function is uncertain. Previous randomized trials and meta-analyses are equivocal, with follow-up limited to 12 months. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, participant- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. A total of 181 patients undergoing elective primary TKA for osteoarthritis were randomized intraoperatively to fat pad excision (removed) or minimal resection (retained). Implants and rehabilitation were standardized. The primary outcome was the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months; the secondary outcome was the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) at three, 12, and 24 months. Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U-tests, and within-group changes over time using Kruskal-Wallis tests. In total, 140 participants were analyzed at 24 months (74 removed, 66 retained; 22% loss to follow-up). RESULTS: Both groups improved significantly across all KOOS subscales and OKS over time (P-values < 0.05), with gains exceeding the minimal clinically important difference on KOOS Pain. There were no significant between-group differences in KOOS or OKS at any time point (P-values > 0.05). The only within-group gain unique to one arm was KOOS Symptoms in the removed group between three and 24 months (P-values < 0.05). The KOOS scores did not improve between 12 and 24 months. CONCLUSION: In this study, excision or preservation of the fat pad did not significantly influence pain or function at two years postoperatively. The absence of change beyond 12 months suggests future trials could shorten follow-up.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT with excellent design (double-blind, within-patient randomized trial) examining patellar component downsizing in PS-TKA, directly applicable to arthroplasty surgeons with clear findings on crepitus rates, published in a high-volume arthroplasty journal.
bullets: Removing or preserving the infrapatellar fat pad during primary TKA produced no difference in pain or function scores at two years.
Both groups improved beyond the minimum clinically important threshold for pain, meaning surgeons can base their fat pad decision on exposure needs rather than outcome concerns.
Scores plateaued after 12 months, suggesting one year is sufficient follow-up for future trials on this question.

candidates.title: Xa Inhibitors Are Associated with an Increased Risk of Manipulation after Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty Compared to Aspirin in a Contemporary Cohort.
candidates.authors_short: McGee AS, Baur AJ, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Aspirin is routinely used for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis following total knee arthroplasty (TKA), though some patients may require more aggressive chemoprophylaxis, now often with Xa inhibitors. There is concern Xa inhibitors may increase bleeding, leading to swelling and stiffness, which can lead to manipulation under anesthesia (MUA). This study compared rates of MUA following primary TKA for patients receiving Xa inhibitors versus aspirin and between Xa inhibitors in a contemporary cohort. METHODS: A database identified 435,789 patients undergoing unilateral primary TKA from 2021 to 2023. During the perioperative window (30 days preoperatively to 3 days postoperatively), 32,778 (7.5%) received rivaroxaban, 53,504 (12.3%) apixaban, and 349,507 (80.2%) aspirin. The incidence of MUA was determined using Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code 27570 within 90 days following TKA. Univariable associations between chemoprophylaxis and MUA were assessed using Chi-square tests. Multivariable associations adjusted for patient demographics, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, and body mass index were assessed using logistic regression with odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) reported. RESULTS: Overall, 13,142 (3.0%) underwent MUA, and this was more common in patients receiving Xa inhibitors versus aspirin (3.9 versus 2.8%, P < 0.001). After adjusting for patient characteristics, Xa inhibitors were associated with higher odds of MUA (OR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.54 to 1.67). In univariable analysis, the rate of MUA was similar between rivaroxaban and apixaban (3.7 versus 3.9%, P = 0.11), though after adjusting for patient characteristics, rivaroxaban was associated with lower odds of MUA compared with apixaban (OR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.83 to 0.95). CONCLUSION: Factor Xa inhibitors are associated with a significantly increased risk of MUA within 90 days of primary TKA compared to aspirin in a contemporary cohort. Unadjusted MUA rates were similar between rivaroxaban and apixaban. Adjusted odds were lower with rivaroxaban.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large multicenter RCT-level systematic review and meta-analysis of PRP timing in rotator cuff repair with 15 RCTs and 1214 patients demonstrating significant retear reduction with intraoperative PRP, directly actionable for surgeons performing ARCR.
bullets: Patients who received factor Xa inhibitors after primary total knee arthroplasty had a 60% higher adjusted odds of needing manipulation under anesthesia within 90 days compared to those on aspirin.
This finding applies to the roughly 1 in 5 total knee arthroplasty patients who require stronger chemoprophylaxis than aspirin, a common scenario in higher-risk patients.
When a Xa inhibitor is necessary, rivaroxaban carried lower adjusted odds of manipulation than apixaban, which may inform agent selection in orthopaedic practice.

candidates.title: Timing of platelet-rich plasma administration in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
candidates.authors_short: Tareen H, Mostafa OES, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated as a biologic adjunct in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (ARCR), yet clinical evidence remains heterogeneous. One potential source of variability is the timing of PRP administration, which may influence tendon-to-bone healing. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of PRP augmentation on structural healing and clinical outcomes following ARCR, with particular evaluation of outcomes according to the timing of PRP administration. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered on PROSPERO. PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL and Web of Science were searched through 19 February 2026. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing PRP augmentation with control in adult patients undergoing ARCR were included. Trials were stratified by timing of PRP administration (intraoperative, post-operative-only or combined). The primary outcome was retears assessed by post-operative imaging at ≥6 months. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. RESULTS: Fifteen RCTs (1214 patients; 647 PRP and 567 control) met inclusion criteria. Overall, PRP administration at ≥6 months was associated with a reduced risk of retears (RR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.40-0.70; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%). Subgroup analysis demonstrated that intraoperative PRP significantly reduced retear rates at ≥6 months (RR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.35-0.68; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%) and ≥12 months (RR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.30-0.91; p = 0.021; I2 = 0%). Post-operative-only PRP did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in retears (RR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.01-8.12; p = 0.54). Absolute risk reduction at ≥6 months was approximately 12%, corresponding to a number needed to treat of 8. Functional outcome scores improved in both PRP and control groups, with significant differences between groups in included studies, but pooled analyses did not demonstrate consistent between-group differences. PRP was not associated with increased complication rates. CONCLUSION: Intraoperative PRP augmentation during ARCR is associated with a statistically significant reduction in retears. The limited post-operative-only PRP protocols do not demonstrate a comparable benefit and preclude a definitive conclusion that efficacy differs according to timing. These findings suggest a potential timing-dependent structural effect of PRP. However, structural improvements did not consistently translate into superior functional outcomes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I.
candidates.score_reasoning: Well-designed RCT from a high-impact journal directly addressing whether fat pad excision in TKA affects outcomes, with 181 patients, blinded design, and 24-month follow-up providing definitive negative finding that is immediately practice-relevant.
bullets: Intraoperative PRP during rotator cuff repair reduces retear rates by roughly half, with a number needed to treat of 8 patients to prevent one retear.
PRP given only after surgery did not significantly reduce retears, suggesting timing of application matters for structural healing.
Despite lower retear rates with intraoperative PRP, functional outcome scores did not consistently improve compared to controls, so the clinical relevance of structural protection remains uncertain.

candidates.title: What matters more in the time to flap: injury-to-flap or definitive-fixation-to-flap?
candidates.authors_short: Mundy LR, Coto SD, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the optimal threshold between injury, first debridement, and fixation-to-flap that minimizes infection risk in adult patients who sustained an open fracture requiring acute flap coverage. METHODS: Design: A retrospective, secondary analysis using data from two prospective randomized controlled trials (XXX and XXX trials) to evaluate infection and time to flap coverage. SETTING: Multinational clinical trial at 25 institutions. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: This secondary analysis included patients 18 years and older, who underwent definitive fracture fixation with an implant, and operative debridement within 72 hours of injury. Patients also had to receive a free or pedicled flap for acute injury management, rather than for wound dehiscence or infection. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Infection rate at 3-months was assessed using Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) criteria with a sensitivity analysis at 12-months. Time from injury-to-flap, first debridement-to-flap and definitive fixation-to-flap intervals were evaluated using multivariate logistic regression models while adjusting for demographic and clinical factors. Included covariates were selected based on a stepwise procedure, using the Akaike Information Criterion, and on their clinical or sociodemographic relevance. RESULTS: The analysis included 138 patients. 32 patients (23.2%) developed an infection and 106 did not (76.8%). The two groups were similar with regards to demographic and injury-related characteristics, with a mean age of 44.9 years (standard deviation [SD] 16.0) in the group of patients with a primary infection versus 44.8 years (SD 16.0) in those who did not develop an infection. Seventy-five percent of patients with a primary infection were male compared to 63.2% in the other group. Mean time to flap was 9.7 days (range 0.0 - 30.0). Multivariate analysis showed that a flap within 7 days following injury (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.09-0.74, p=0.01) or first debridement (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.12-0.89, p<0.05) was associated with lower rates of infection, compared to those who underwent a flap in 7 days or greater following injury or first debridement. Time from injury to flap (OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.91-1.03, p = 0.343) and time from fixation to flap (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.95-1.10, p = 0.699) were not associated with lower rates of infection. CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests that limiting the time from injury and first debridement to flap to less than 7 days was associated with decreased risk of infection. However, infection was not found to be associated with time from definitive fixation-to-flap. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large database retrospective cohort study (435,789 patients) with significant clinical relevance showing Xa inhibitors increase MUA risk after TKA versus aspirin, directly informing VTE prophylaxis decision-making in arthroplasty practice.
bullets: In adults with open fractures requiring flap coverage, getting the flap done within 7 days of injury or first debridement cuts infection risk by roughly 70%.
The clock that matters starts at injury and first debridement, not at definitive fixation, so delays in plating do not independently drive infection.
For open fractures needing soft tissue coverage, surgeons should prioritize flap timing from day of injury, not from when hardware goes in.

candidates.title: Operative Strategies for Treating Tibial Plateau Fractures in Patients Aged 55 Years and Older: A Five-Year Comparison of Acute Total Knee Arthroplasty with Open Reduction and Internal Fixation, Conversion Total Knee Arthroplasty, and Total Knee Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis.
candidates.authors_short: Wahid M, Bellamy J, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare outcomes of acute total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for tibial plateau fracture in patients aged 55 years and older with matched patients undergoing open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), conversion TKA after failed ORIF, and primary TKA for osteoarthritis. METHODS: Design: Retrospective cohort study with propensity score matching. SETTING: Federated multi-institutional electronic health records database (TriNetX United States Collaborative Network). PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged ≥55 years with tibial plateau fracture treated with acute TKA, ORIF, or conversion TKA after failed ORIF were identified. A separate cohort undergoing primary TKA for osteoarthritis without fracture history was identified as a non-traumatic comparator. The study period was restricted to January 1, 2005 through December 31, 2020 to ensure a minimum of five years of potential follow-up for all included patients. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome was revision surgery at 5 years, defined as conversion to TKA after ORIF and as revision TKA after arthroplasty. Secondary outcomes were a composite "return to the operating room (OR)" outcome (selected major reoperations), periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), surgical site infection (SSI), aseptic loosening, manipulation under anesthesia (MUA), and periprosthetic fracture. Three 1:1 propensity score-matched comparisons were performed (acute TKA versus ORIF; acute versus conversion TKA; acute TKA versus primary TKA for osteoarthritis), with risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated. Subgroup analyses were stratified by age (55-70 years; ≥70 years). RESULTS: After matching, 1,321 patients per cohort were compared in the primary acute TKA versus ORIF analysis. Mean age was 66.1 years in the acute TKA cohort and 66.6 years in the ORIF cohort (range, 55 to 90 in both), and 65.3% and 66.7%, respectively, were female. Acute TKA had higher 5-year revision rates than ORIF (7.0% versus 0.8%; RR 8.36, 95% CI 4.50-15.56; P < 0.001) and elevated PJI rates (6.2% versus 1.3%; RR 4.82, 95% CI 2.88-8.09; P < 0.001). Return to OR rates did not differ significantly between acute TKA and ORIF (25.6% versus 23.5%; RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.95-1.25; P = 0.21). Revision did not differ between acute and conversion TKA (9.0% versus 10.0%; RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.58-1.35; P = 0.589) but was higher after acute TKA than after primary TKA for osteoarthritis (7.4% versus 3.5%; RR 2.12, 95% CI 1.48-3.00; P < 0.001). Revision was higher after acute TKA than ORIF in patients aged 55-70 years (9.3% versus 1.7%; RR 5.41, 95% CI 2.80-10.48; P < 0.001) and was not reportable in those aged ≥70 years owing to small cell counts. CONCLUSIONS: In patients aged 55 years and older, acute TKA for tibial plateau fracture was associated with higher risks of revision and complications compared with ORIF. Revision and complication rates after acute TKA were comparable with those after conversion TKA following failed ORIF but higher than those after primary TKA for osteoarthritis. Acute TKA should be reserved for patients at highest risk of ORIF failure requiring subsequent conversion to TKA. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective multicenter 10-year cohort study of 675 hips evaluating vitamin E-infused HXLPE cup with 98.7% survivorship and excellent Harris Hip Scores, providing important long-term durability data for implant selection.
bullets: In patients 55 and older with tibial plateau fractures, acute TKA carried a much higher 5-year revision rate than ORIF (7% vs 0.8%) and nearly five times the rate of periprosthetic joint infection.
Revision rates after acute TKA were similar to those after conversion TKA for failed ORIF, meaning upfront TKA does not spare patients from the complication burden of a staged approach.
Acute TKA for tibial plateau fracture should be reserved for patients at high risk of ORIF failure, as ORIF remains the lower-risk option for most patients in this age group.

candidates.title: Nonoperative Management Deserves Consideration for Select Patients with Valgus-Impacted Femoral Neck Fractures.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: The valgus-impacted femoral neck fracture is unique among hip fractures. Patients are often relatively comfortable, and the fracture pattern is inherently more stable than other femoral neck fracture types. In situ fixation remains the default treatment for most surgeons, and this remains a reasonable approach, particularly for patients unable to reliably protect their weight-bearing. However, multiple randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses have revealed that, when surgery is chosen, arthroplasty carries a lower risk of reoperation and implant-related complications than fixation, with no difference in mortality. Additionally, nonoperative management has achieved rates of uneventful healing comparable with those of fixation in appropriately selected patients who were able to protect their weight-bearing, and delayed arthroplasty after failed nonoperative treatment has not been associated with excess morbidity compared with acute arthroplasty across measured outcomes. Given that fixation in situ may not have dramatically better efficacy than nonoperative care and that failed nonoperative management can be salvaged with delayed arthroplasty without excess morbidity, we propose that nonoperative management is a reasonable initial treatment for select patients. The best candidates are patients who are cognitively intact, living independently, and medically stable and who are reasonably comfortable and capable of mobilizing while protecting their weight-bearing. Close clinical and radiographic follow-up is required, with a low threshold for conversion to arthroplasty in the setting of uncontrolled pain, poor mobilization, or radiographic evidence of loss of reduction. Dementia, high comorbidity burden, and assisted living status are associated with failure of nonoperative management. In all circumstances, both fixation and acute arthroplasty remain valid alternative strategies. We advocate a shared decision-making approach that accounts for the risks and benefits of all treatment strategies as well as patient factors.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS roadmap article from NIH-funded AJRR collaborative outlining registry-nested trial infrastructure representing a paradigm shift in arthroplasty research methodology, highly relevant for understanding future evidence generation.
bullets: In cognitively intact, independently living, medically stable patients with valgus-impacted femoral neck fractures, nonoperative management achieves healing rates comparable to in situ fixation when weight-bearing precautions can be reliably followed.
If nonoperative management fails, delayed arthroplasty carries no excess morbidity compared to acute arthroplasty, making it a viable salvage option.
Dementia, high comorbidity burden, and assisted living status predict failure of nonoperative management and should steer surgeons toward operative treatment upfront.

candidates.title: Fracture Care in Older Individuals.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS review challenging the default surgical management of valgus-impacted femoral neck fractures by synthesizing RCT and meta-analysis evidence supporting nonoperative management in select patients, potentially practice-changing.
bullets: Older patients sustaining fractures face higher rates of complications, mortality, and functional decline compared to younger patients with similar injuries.
Orthopaedic surgeons should account for bone quality, comorbidities, and functional baseline when selecting fixation strategies in elderly fracture patients.
Coordinated perioperative care, including medical comanagement and early mobilisation, improves outcomes in older adults treated for fractures.

candidates.title: Safety and Clinical Impact of Emergency Department Closed Reduction for Gartland Type III Supracondylar Humerus Fractures.
candidates.authors_short: Kelley NH, Carroll CJ, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric type 3 supracondylar humerus fractures (SCHFs) are typically immobilized in situ before definitive operative fixation because of concern for neurovascular injury during closed reduction. This study assesses the safety and clinical outcomes of emergency department (ED) closed reduction versus in situ splinting for type 3 SCHFs before definitive fixation. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of all pediatric extension-type 3 SCHFs that underwent closed reduction versus no reduction by orthopaedic surgery residents in the ED at a single Level 1 trauma center over a 5-year period. Data included pre- and postreduction neurovascular examinations, multiple radiographic parameters, durations of time between injury, consult, and reduction to the operating room (OR), total operative time, and OR fluoroscopy duration. RESULTS: Of 112 patients, 54 underwent closed reduction (CR) while 58 were not reduced (NR). Nine (20%) patients in the CR group and 9 (18%) patients in the NR group had abnormal neurological exams on presentation. Four (8%) patients in the CR group and 2 (4%) patients in the NR group had abnormal vascular exams. All 4 patients who underwent closed reduction had improved vascular exams from Doppler-able to palpable radial pulses (P=0.12). No vascular injuries occurred with closed reduction. Importantly, 6 patients in the NR group with initial normal exams developed abnormal neurological deficits while awaiting surgical fixation (P=0.03). The CR group demonstrated significantly improved radiographic parameters postreduction, including AP and lateral displacement, anterior humeral line displacement, lateral Baumann angle, and hourglass angle. The time from consult or reduction to OR was significantly less for the NR group compared with the CR group (9.83 vs. 13.45 h; P<0.01). The time from injury to the OR was also significantly less in the NR group (21.0 vs. 17.0 h; P=0.02). The CR group trended towards shorter operative times (33 vs. 40 min; P=0.15). CONCLUSION: Closed reduction of pediatric type 3 SCHFs in the ED by orthopaedic surgery residents is safe and can improve both neurovascular deficits and radiographic fracture alignment. As most pediatric extremity fractures undergo closed reduction in the ED, type 3 SCHFs should not be considered an exception. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III-retrospective comparative study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Novel retrospective comparative study of 221 ACLRs showing extensor mechanism grafts (BPTB/QT) associated with 2.45x higher odds of thigh muscle injury in first year, directly relevant to graft selection counseling for athletes.
bullets: Emergency department closed reduction of Gartland III supracondylar fractures by orthopaedic residents caused no vascular injuries and improved pulseless limbs from Doppler-only to palpable radial pulses.
Six children in the splinted-in-place group developed new neurological deficits while waiting for the operating room, compared to none in the closed reduction group.
ED closed reduction is safe for Gartland III supracondylar fractures in children and should be performed routinely rather than avoided out of concern for neurovascular risk.

candidates.title: What Are the Long-term Outcomes of Periacetabular Osteotomy in a United States Cohort?
candidates.authors_short: Maroyan A, Mendola LC, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) is an effective and common hip-preserving procedure used to treat symptomatic acetabular dysplasia of the hip. Evidence regarding long-term outcomes after PAO remains limited. Information regarding long-term outcomes may be important in developing reasonable expectations for both patients and surgeons to facilitate effective therapeutic decision-making. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) What is the likelihood of long-term hip preservation and the level of pain at a minimum of 25 years of follow-up after PAO? (2) What clinical and radiographic factors were associated with patients having a poor result, which we defined either as having THA or a WOMAC score of ≥ 10 points at the most recent survey? (3) What were the outcome scores of patients who underwent THA after PAO, and how did these scores compare to the scores of the preserved hips and to the scores of age-related norms? METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated the cohort of the first 142 patients (171 hips) who underwent PAO performed by one surgeon to treat symptomatic dysplasia between 1991 and 1998. Twenty-three percent (33 of 142) of patients (37 hips) were lost to follow-up. This included six patients (6 hips) who had died, 23 patients (26 hips) who could not be located, and four patients (5 hips) who did not complete questionnaires. Seventy-seven percent (109 of 142) of eligible patients (134 hips) returned complete questionnaires at a median (range) of 27 years (25 to 33) after PAO. Our analyzed group included 87% female patients (95 patients, 117 hips) and 13% male patients (14 patients, 17 hips). The median (range) age at surgery was 25 years (9 to 45). The median (range) time of review after PAO was 27 years (25 to 33). The 53 hips that had undergone THA were reviewed at a median (range) of 11 years (1 to 28) after the THA. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to assess survivorship free from conversion to THA. Hips were postoperatively evaluated using the pain subscale of the WOMAC index. We characterized a poor clinical outcome as either having a preserved hip with a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10 or undergoing THA. All patients who were analyzed returned questionnaires; some were seen in person with images. Factors associated with a patient having a high (poor) WOMAC score for pain or undergoing THA were evaluated using a multinomial logistic regression model using generalized estimating equations. RESULTS: Of patients analyzed, 60% (81 of 134) of hips remained preserved. Forty percent (53 of 134) of hips had undergone THA at a median of 22 years after PAO. The survivorship free from conversion to THA at 25 years after PAO was 70% (95% confidence interval [CI] 62% to 78%), and the median (range) level of pain was 1 (0 to 20) of 20 points. After controlling for potentially confounding variables including sex, preoperative lateral center-edge angle and anterior center-edge angle, and postoperative lateral center-edge angle, we found that the following factors were associated with increased odds of having either a poor (≥ 10 points) WOMAC pain score or conversion to THA: preoperative joint space width ≤ 2 mm (HR 7.3 [95% CI 2.8 to 19.2]), labral tear noted intraoperatively (HR 2.8 [95% CI 1.3 to 5.8]), age at surgery > 21 years and < 35 years (HR 2.6 [95% CI 1.1 to 5.9]), and age at surgery ≥ 35 years (HR 3.4 [95% CI 1.1 to 11.0]). In patients who underwent THA, the median (range) WOMAC score was 1 (0 to 20) (lower scores represent less pain and better function), the median (range) modified Harris hip score was 85 (7 to 91) points (higher scores represent less pain and better function), and the median (range) HOOS pain score was 95 (0 to 100). The mean University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity level score for the THA group was 6. In general, these scores did not differ by clinically important margins when compared with the hips that had not undergone THA or compared with age-related score norms. CONCLUSION: While a majority of hips can be preserved with good function at a mean of 27 years after PAO, our findings suggest that surgery should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of symptomatic dysplasia is made, given that older age at the time of surgery was independently associated with later THA or a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10. If a patient develops painful arthrosis after a PAO, THA should be offered and expected to provide function comparable to age-related norms. Prospective registry-based multicenter studies of patients treated for symptomatic hip dysplasia are indicated to improve outcomes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE LEVEL: III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Long-term outcomes study of 134 PAO patients at minimum 25 years follow-up with 73.9% hip preservation rate providing rare and clinically valuable information for counseling patients about hip preservation surgery.
bullets: At 27-year follow-up after periacetabular osteotomy for hip dysplasia, 70% of hips survived without conversion to total hip arthroplasty and preserved hips had near-normal pain scores.

Narrowed preoperative joint space of 2 mm or less, intraoperative labral tear, and age over 21 at surgery were each independently associated with worse long-term outcomes or conversion to arthroplasty.

Patients who eventually required total hip arthroplasty after periacetabular osteotomy achieved pain and function scores comparable to age-matched population norms, so arthroplasty should be offered without hesitation when dysplastic hips develop painful arthrosis.
